description: A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust. Magma under pressure rises through it and becomes lava. Here is why the Earth “spits.”

hero.hook: Under our feet, the Earth is not still. Sometimes it opens a window of fire.

blocks.text: A volcano is not just a mountain that spits fire. It is an opening in the Earth's outer shell. Through it rises **magma**: a mix of molten rock and gas under high pressure. Once out in the open air, that magma becomes **lava**.

To understand an eruption, you have to look below the surface: the planet's inner heat, the movement of the plates, and the way gas drives the pressure up, a little like a bottle of soda that has been shaken.

The Earth is made of layers. At the surface, the **crust** is a rigid shell, **5 to 70 km** thick. Below it the **mantle** reaches down to about **2,900 km**. The mantle is mostly solid, but over very long stretches of time it can flow very slowly, like ultra-thick honey.

blocks.caption: An eruption: magma rising all the way to the surface

blocks.text: This inner heat makes material rise and sink again: these are **convection currents**. They push the big pieces of crust we call plates. This is [[Plate tectonics]]: the Earth's surface is cut into plates that pull apart, collide, or slide against one another.
Some very fast rises bring up diamonds formed more than **150 km** down. They have no time to change on the way.

At the ocean [[ridges]], the plates pull apart and magma rises easily. In a [[subduction]] zone, one plate dives under another and drags water down with it. That water lowers the melting point of the rock: magma forms, then rises.

sections.title: Under our feet, nothing stands still

blocks.text: Rock does not melt just “because it is hot.” Three triggers matter: a rise in temperature, a drop in pressure, or the arrival of water. Once it has formed, magma is less dense than the rock around it. So it tries to rise, a little like an air bubble in water.

Often it stops first in a **magma chamber**, a reservoir a few kilometers below the surface. There, the dissolved gases turn into bubbles as the pressure falls. When the rock “plug” above can no longer hold, the eruption begins.

The eruption of **Tambora** in **1815**, in Indonesia, was so powerful that it cooled the world's climate. **1816** was nicknamed “the year without a summer,” with disastrous harvests in Europe and North America.

Not all eruptions are alike. Everything depends on the **viscosity** of the magma, that is, on whether it is runny or sticky. Runny magma, as in **Hawaii** or at Piton de la Fournaise on Reunion Island, lets the gas escape. The lava flows: an **effusive** eruption.

Sticky magma traps the gas. The pressure builds, then everything blows. Ash, blocks, and [[pyroclastic flows]] (burning clouds of gas and ash that race down the slopes) can then wreck the surroundings. That is the style of volcanoes like **Mount St. Helens** in the United States or **Pinatubo** in the Philippines.

A volcano can also stay quiet for centuries. In **AD 79**, **Vesuvius**, near Naples, buried Pompeii under ash. About **80%** of the world's volcanic activity happens under the oceans, far from our eyes.

Volcanoes shaped the Earth's early atmosphere by releasing gas. Their ash also enriches the soil: many fertile farming regions sit at the foot of active volcanoes. But a very large eruption can send sulfur particles high into the atmosphere and cool the climate for months.

Some sites, such as the Yellowstone [[supervolcano]] in the United States, are watched closely. Under the sea, near the ridges, [[black smokers]] spew out scalding fluids rich in minerals. Whole ecosystems live there without sunlight, fed by the chemistry of the hot springs.
Volcanoes push out magma under pressure, above all at the boundaries of the tectonic plates. The viscosity of the magma decides whether an eruption flows quietly or explodes.
